idiom_name: options parameter typed as an interface with optional properties, merged with defaults
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits the options-object idiom and adds type safety around it: an interface declares the optional properties, defaults are merged at the single construction point, and Partial<T> / Readonly<Required<T>> express "the caller supplies a subset" and "the built value is complete" without a builder class. Reach for a builder class when clauses accumulate (TypeORM's SelectQueryBuilder, Knex) or when the chain itself must be typed; for a fixed set of settings the options object is shorter and just as safe.
pitfalls: Spreading a partial object over defaults does not make the result checked: the annotation only holds if the defaults cover every key, and under exactOptionalPropertyTypes an explicit undefined is not the same as an omitted key.
Structural typing accepts extra properties from a variable (only object literals are excess-property-checked), so a typo can survive once the options object is assembled in stages.

variants.name: Fluent builder with compile-time step tracking
variants.idiom_name: generic builder class ConfigBuilder<T extends Partial<Config> = {}> with build(this: ConfigBuilder<Config>)
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript can move the builder's completeness check into the type system: the builder carries the already-provided keys as a type parameter, each step returns the builder with that parameter intersected with the new key, and build(this: ConfigBuilder<Config>) is only callable once every required key is present, so an incomplete chain is a compile error instead of an exception. The runtime side stays an ordinary mutable fluent builder; prefer the options object when there are no ordering or validation requirements and no chain to type.
pitfalls: The this constraint is erased at runtime: a caller who bypasses the chain (as any, or a config assembled from JSON) still gets an incomplete value, so keep a runtime check on that boundary.
Async steps break the typed chain - a step returning Promise<Builder> produces nested promises and loses the accumulated state type - so keep steps synchronous and await the finished value.
The state type is invisible in hover text on long chains, and this as any casts hide mistakes inside the step implementations themselves.
